{{Short description|Mathematical concept named for Ernst Witt}}
In [[mathematics]], a '''Witt vector''' is an [[infinite sequence]] of elements of a [[commutative ring|commutative]] [[ring (mathematics)|ring]]. [[Ernst Witt]] showed how to put a ring [[mathematical structure|structure]] on the set of Witt vectors, in such a way that the ring of Witt vectors <math>W(\mathbb{F}_p)</math> over the [[finite field|finite]] [[field (mathematics)|field]] of [[prime number|prime]] order ''p'' is [[isomorphic]] to <math>\mathbb{Z}_p</math>, the ring of [[p-adic integers|''p''-adic integers]]. They have a highly non-intuitive structure<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|last=Fisher|first=Benji|date=1999|title=Notes on Witt Vectors: a motivated approach|url=http://www.claymath.org/sites/default/files/brinon_witt.pdf|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190112130142/http://www.claymath.org/sites/default/files/brinon_witt.pdf|archive-date=12 January 2019}}</ref> upon first glance because their additive and multiplicative structure depends on an [[infinite set]] of recursive formulas which do not behave like addition and multiplication formulas for standard ''p''-adic integers. 

The main idea<ref name=":0" /> behind Witt vectors is that instead of using the standard ''p''-adic expansion<blockquote><math>a = a_0+a_1p+a_2p^2 + \cdots</math></blockquote>to represent an element in <math>\mathbb{Z}_p</math>, an expansion using the [[Teichmüller character]] can be considered instead;<blockquote><math>\omega: \mathbb{F}_p^* \to \mathbb{Z}_p^*</math>,</blockquote>which is a group morphism sending each element in the [[solution set]] of <math>x^{p-1}-1</math> in <math>\mathbb{F}_p</math> to an element in the solution set of <math>x^{p-1}-1</math> in <math>\mathbb{Z}_p</math>. That is, the elements in <math>\mathbb{Z}_p</math> can be expanded out in terms of [[roots of unity]] instead of as profinite elements in <math>\prod \mathbb{F}_p</math>. We also set <math>\omega(0)=0</math>, which defines an injective multiplicative map <math>\omega: \mathbb{F}_p \to \mathbb{Z}_p</math> sending elements of <math>\mathbb{F}_p</math> to roots of <math>x^p-x</math> in <math>\mathbb{Z}_p</math>.  A ''p''-adic integer can then be expressed as an infinite sum<blockquote><math>a = \omega(a_0) + \omega(a_1)p + \omega(a_2)p^2 + \cdots</math>,</blockquote>which gives a Witt vector<blockquote><math>(a_0, a_1, a_2,\ldots)\in W(\mathbb{F}_p)= (\mathbb{F}_p)^{\mathbb{N}}</math>.</blockquote>Then, the non-trivial additive and multiplicative structure in Witt vectors comes from using this map to give <math>W(\mathbb{F}_p)</math> an additive and multiplicative structure such that <math>\omega</math> induces a commutative ring [[homomorphism]].

== History ==

In the 19th century, [[Ernst Eduard Kummer]] studied [[cyclic extension|cyclic]] [[field extension|extensions]] of fields as part of his work on [[Fermat's Last Theorem]]. This led to the subject known as [[Kummer theory]]. Let <math>k</math> be a field containing a primitive <math>n</math>-th root of unity. Kummer theory classifies [[degree of a field extension|degree]] <math>n</math> cyclic field extensions <math>K</math> of <math>k</math>. Such fields are in [[bijection]] with order <math>n</math> [[cyclic group|cyclic]] [[group (mathematics)|group]]s <math>\Delta \subseteq k^\times / (k^\times)^n</math>, where <math>\Delta</math> corresponds to <math>K=k(\sqrt[n]{\Delta}\,)</math>.

But suppose that <math>k</math> has [[characteristic (algebra)|characteristic]] <math>p</math>. The problem of studying degree <math>p</math> extensions of <math>k</math>, or more generally degree <math>p^n</math> extensions, may appear superficially similar to Kummer theory. However, in this situation, <math>k</math> cannot contain a primitive <math>p</math>-th root of unity. If <math>x</math> is a <math>p</math>-th root of unity in <math>k</math>, then it satisfies <math>x^p=1</math>. But consider the expression <math>(x-1)^p=0</math>. By expanding using [[binomial coefficient]]s, the operation of raising to the <math>p</math>-th power, known here as the [[Frobenius homomorphism]], introduces the factor <math>p</math> to every coefficient except the first and the last, and so modulo <math>p</math> these equations are the same. Therefore <math>x = 1</math>. Consequently, Kummer theory is never applicable to extensions whose degree is divisible by the characteristic.

The case where the characteristic divides the degree is today called [[Artin–Schreier theory]] because the first progress was made by Artin and Schreier. Their initial motivation was the [[Artin–Schreier theorem]], which characterizes the [[real closed field]]s as those whose [[absolute Galois group]] has order two.<ref>Artin, Emil and Schreier, Otto, ''Über eine Kennzeichnung der reell abgeschlossenen Körper'', Abh. Math. Sem. Hamburg '''3''' (1924).</ref> This inspired them to ask what other fields had [[finite group|finite]] absolute Galois groups. In the midst of [[mathematical proof|proving]] that no other such fields exist, they proved that degree <math>p</math> extensions of a field <math>k</math> of characteristic <math>p</math> were the same as [[splitting field]]s of ''Artin–Schreier polynomials''. These are by definition of the form <math>x^p-x-a.</math> By repeating their construction, they described degree <math>p^2</math> extensions. [[Abraham Adrian Albert]] used this idea to describe degree <math>p^n</math> extensions. Each repetition entailed complicated algebraic conditions to ensure that the field extension was [[normal extension|normal]].<ref>A. A. Albert, ''Cyclic fields of degree'' <math>p^n</math> over <math>F</math> of characteristic <math>p</math>, Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. '''40''' (1934).</ref>

Schmid<ref>Schmid, H. L., ''Zyklische algebraische Funktionenkörper vom Grad'' ''p<sup>n</sup>'' ''über endlichen Konstantenkörper der Charakteristik'' ''p'', Crelle '''175''' (1936).</ref> generalized further to non-commutative cyclic algebras of degree <math>p^n</math>. In the process of doing so, certain [[polynomial]]s related to the addition of <math>p</math>-adic integers appeared. Witt seized on these polynomials. By using them systematically, he was able to give simple and unified constructions of degree <math>p^n</math> field extensions and cyclic algebras. Specifically, he introduced a ring now called <math>W_n(k)</math>, the '''ring of <math>n</math>-truncated <math>p</math>-typical Witt vectors'''. This ring has <math>k</math> as a [[quotient ring|quotient]], and it comes with an operator <math>F</math> which is called the Frobenius operator since it reduces to the Frobenius operator on <math>k</math>. Witt observed that the degree <math>p^n</math> analog of Artin–Schreier polynomials is

:<math>F(x)-x-a</math>,

where <math>a \in W_n(k)</math>. To complete the analogy with Kummer theory, define <math>\wp</math> to be the operator <math>x \mapsto F(x)-x.</math> Then the degree <math>p^n</math> extensions of <math>k</math> are in bijective correspondence with cyclic [[subgroup]]s <math>\Delta \subseteq W_n(k) / \wp(W_n(k))</math> of order <math>p^n</math>, where <math>\Delta</math> corresponds to the field <math>k(\wp^{-1}(\Delta))</math>.

==Motivation==

Any <math>p</math>-adic integer (an element of <math>\Z_p</math>, not to be confused with <math>\Z/p\Z=\mathbb{F}_p</math>) can be written as a [[power series]] <math>a_0+a_1p^1+a_2p^2+\cdots</math>, where the <math>a_i</math> are usually taken from the [[integer]] interval <math>[0,p-1]=\{0,1,2,\ldots,p-1\}</math>. It can be difficult to provide an [[algebraic expression]] for addition and multiplication using this representation, as one faces the problem of carrying between digits. However, taking representative coefficients <math>a_i\in [0,p-1]</math> is only one of many choices, and [[Kurt Hensel|Hensel]] himself (the creator of <math>p</math>-adic numbers) suggested the roots of unity in the field as representatives{{Citation needed|date=April 2026}}. These representatives are therefore the number <math>0</math> together with the <math>(p-1)^{\text{st}}</math> roots of unity; that is, the solutions of <math>x^p - x = 0</math> in <math>\Z_p</math>, so that <math>a_i=a_i^p</math>. This choice extends naturally to ring extensions of <math>\Z_p</math> in which the [[residue field]] is enlarged to <math>\mathbb{F}_q</math> with <math>q=p^f</math>, some power of <math>p</math>. Indeed, it is these fields (the [[field of fractions|fields of fractions]] of the rings) that motivated Hensel's choice. Now the representatives are the <math>q</math> solutions in the field to <math>x^q-x=0</math>. Call the field <math>\Z_p(\eta)</math>, with <math>\eta</math> an appropriate primitive <math>(q-1)^{\text{th}}</math> root of unity (over <math>\Z_p</math>). The representatives are then <math>0</math> and <math>\eta^i</math> for <math>0\leq i\leq q-2</math>. Since these representatives form a multiplicative set they can be thought of as characters. Some thirty years after Hensel's works, [[Oswald Teichmüller|Teichmüller]] studied these characters, which now bear his name, and this led him to a characterisation of the structure of the whole field in terms of the residue field. These '''Teichmüller representatives''' can be identified with the elements of the finite field <math>\mathbb{F}_q</math> of order <math>q</math> by taking residues modulo <math>p</math> in <math>\Z_p(\eta)</math>, and elements of <math>\mathbb{F}_q^\times</math> are taken to their representatives by the [[Teichmüller character]] <math>\omega:\mathbb{F}_q^\times\to\Z_p(\eta)^\times</math>. This operation identifies the set of integers in <math>\Z_p(\eta)</math> with infinite sequences of elements of <math>\omega(\mathbb{F}_q^\times)\cup\{0\}</math>.

Taking those representatives, the expressions for addition and multiplication can be written in closed form. The following problem (stated for the simplest case: <math>q=p</math>): given two infinite sequences of elements of <math>\omega(\mathbb{F}_p^\times)\cup\{0\}</math>, describe their sum and product as ''p''-adic integers explicitly. This problem was solved by Witt using Witt vectors.{{Citation needed|date=January 2025}}

===Detailed motivational sketch===

The ring of <math>p</math>-adic integers <math>\Z_p</math> is derived from the finite field <math>\mathbb{F}_p=\Z /p\Z</math> using a construction which naturally generalizes to the Witt vector construction.

The ring <math>\Z_p</math> of ''p''-adic integers can be understood as the [[inverse limit]] of the rings <math>\Z /p^i\Z</math> taken along the projections. Specifically, it consists of the sequences <math>(n_0,n_1,\ldots)</math> with <math>n_i\in\Z/p^{i+1}\Z</math>, such that <math>n_j\equiv n_i\bmod p^{i+1}</math> for <math>j\ge i</math>. That is, each successive element of the sequence is equal to the previous elements modulo a lower power of ''p''; this is the inverse limit of the projections <math>\Z/p^{i+1}\Z\to\Z/p^i\Z</math>.

The elements of <math>\Z_p</math> can be expanded as [[formal power series|(formal) power series]] in <math>p</math>

:<math>a_0+a_1p^1+a_2p^2+\cdots</math>,

where the coefficients <math>a_i</math> are taken from the integer interval <math>[0,p-1]=\{0,1,\ldots,p-1\}</math>. This power series usually will not converge in <math>\R</math> using the standard metric on the [[real number|reals]], but it will converge in <math>\Z_p</math> with the [[p-adic metric|''p''-adic metric]].

Letting <math>a+b</math> be denoted by <math>c</math>, the following definition can be considered for addition:

:<math>\begin{align}
c_0 &\equiv a_0+b_0 && \bmod p \\
c_0+c_1 p &\equiv (a_0+b_0) + (a_1 +b_1)p && \bmod p^2 \\
c_0+c_1 p+c_2 p^2 &\equiv (a_0+b_0) + (a_1 +b_1)p+(a_2+b_2) p^2 &&\bmod p^3
\end{align}</math>

and a similar definition for multiplication can be made. However, this is not a closed formula, since the new coefficients need not be in the allowed set <math>[0,p-1]</math>; take for instance when <math>a_0, b_0 > p/2</math>. In general, one must carry powers of <math>p</math> to simplify the given sum into a form with coefficients in the allowed set.

==== Representing elements in F<sub>''p''</sub> as elements in the ring of Witt vectors W(F<sub>''p''</sub>) ====
There is a coefficient subset of <math>\Z_p</math> which does yield closed formulas, the '''Teichmüller representatives''': zero together with the <math>(p-1)^{\text{th}}</math> roots of unity. They can be explicitly calculated (in terms of the original coefficient representatives <math>[0,p-1]</math>)  as roots of <math>x^{p-1}-1=0</math> through [[Hensel lifting]], the ''p''-adic version of [[Newton's method]]. For example, in <math>\Z_5</math>, to calculate the representative of 2, one starts by finding the unique solution of <math>x^4-1=0</math> in <math>\Z/25\Z</math> with <math>x\equiv2\bmod5</math>; one gets 7. Repeating this in <math>\Z/125\Z</math>, with the conditions <math>x^4-1=0</math> and <math>x\equiv7\bmod25</math>, gives 57, and so on; the resulting Teichmüller representative of 2, denoted <math>\omega(2)</math>, is the sequence<blockquote><math>\omega(2)=(2,7,57,\ldots)\in W(\mathbb{F}_5)</math>.</blockquote>The existence of a lift in each step is guaranteed by the [[greatest common divisor]] <math>(x^{p-1}-1,(p-1)x^{p-2})=1</math> in every <math>\Z/p^n\Z</math>.

This algorithm shows that for every <math>j\in[0,p-1]</math>, there is one Teichmüller representative with <math>a_0=j</math>, which is denoted <math>\omega(j)</math>. This defines the [[Teichmüller character]] <math>\omega:\mathbb{F}_p^*\to\Z_p^*</math> as a (multiplicative) [[group homomorphism]], which moreover satisfies <math>m\circ \omega=\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{F}_p}</math> if one lets <math>m:\Z_p\to \Z_p/p\Z_p \cong \mathbb{F}_p</math> denote the canonical projection. Note however that <math>\omega</math> is ''not'' additive, as the sum need not be a representative. Despite this, if <math>\omega(k) \equiv \omega(i)+\omega(j)\bmod p</math> in <math>\Z_p,</math> then <math>i+j=k</math> in <math>\mathbb{F}_p.</math>

==== Representing elements in Z<sub>''p''</sub> as elements in the ring of Witt vectors W(F<sub>''p''</sub>) ====
Because of this one-to-one correspondence given by <math>\omega</math>, one can expand every ''p''-adic integer as a power series in ''p'' with coefficients taken from the Teichmüller representatives. An explicit algorithm can be given, as follows. Write the Teichmüller representative as <math>\omega(t_0)=t_0+t_1p^1+t_2p^2+\cdots</math>. Then, if one has some arbitrary ''p''-adic integer of the form <math>x=x_0+x_1p^1+x_2p^2+\cdots </math>, one takes the difference <math>x-\omega(x_0)=x'_1p^1+x'_2p^2+\cdots</math>, leaving a value divisible by <math>p</math>. Hence, <math>x-\omega(x_0)=0\bmod p</math>. The process is then repeated, subtracting <math>\omega(x'_1)p</math> and proceed likewise. This yields a sequence of congruences

:<math>\begin{align}x&\equiv\omega(x_0)&&\bmod p\\x&\equiv\omega(x_0)+\omega(x'_1)p&& \bmod p^2\\&\cdots\end{align}</math>

so that 

:<math>x\equiv\sum_{j=0}^i\omega(\bar{x}_j)p^j\bmod p^{i+1}</math>

and <math>i' > i</math> implies 

:<math>\sum_{j = 0}^{i'} \omega(\bar{x}_j)p^j \equiv \sum_{j=0}^i \omega(\bar{x}_j)p^j \bmod p^{i+1}</math>

for 

:<math>\bar{x}_i:=m\left(\frac{x-\sum_{j=0}^{i-1}\omega(\bar{x}_j)p^j}{p^i}\right)</math>.

This obtains a power series for each residue of ''<math>x</math>'' modulo powers of ''<math>p</math>'', but with coefficients in the Teichmüller representatives rather than <math>\{0,\ldots,p-1\}</math>. 

:<math>\sum_{j=0}^\infty\omega(\bar{x}_j)p^j=x </math>,

since 

:<math>p^{i+1}\mid x-\sum_{j=0}^i\omega(\bar{x}_j)p^j</math>

for all <math>i</math> as <math>i\to\infty</math>, so the difference tends to 0 with respect to the ''p''-adic metric. The resulting coefficients will typically differ from the <math>a_i</math> modulo <math>p^i</math> except the first one.

==== Additional properties of elements in the ring of Witt vectors motivating general definition ====
The Teichmüller coefficients have the key additional property that <math>\omega(\bar{x}_i)^p=\omega(\bar{x}_i),</math> which is missing for the numbers in <math>[0,p-1]</math>. This can be used to describe addition, as follows. Consider the equation <math display="inline">c = a+b</math> in <math display="inline">\mathbb{Z}_p</math> and let the coefficients <math display="inline">a_i, b_i, c_i \in \mathbb{Z}_p</math> now be as in the Teichmüller expansion. Since the Teichmüller character is not additive, <math>c_0=a_0+b_0</math> is not true in <math>\Z_p</math>, but it holds in <math>\mathbb{F}_p</math>, as the first congruence implies. In particular, 

:<math>c_0^p\equiv(a_0+b_0)^p\bmod p^2</math>

and thus

:<math>c_0-a_0-b_0\equiv(a_0+b_0)^p-a_0-b_0\equiv\binom{p}{1}a_0^{p-1}b_0+\cdots+\binom{p}{p-1}a_0b_0^{p-1}\bmod p^2 </math>.

Since the binomial coefficient <math>\binom{p}{i}</math> is divisible by <math>p</math>, this gives

:<math>c_1\equiv a_1+b_1-a_0^{p-1}b_0-\frac{p-1}{2}a_0^{p-2}b_0^2-\cdots-a_0b_0^{p-1}\bmod p</math>.

This completely determines <math>c_1</math> by the lift. Moreover, the congruence modulo <math>p</math> indicates that the calculation can actually be done in <math>\mathbb{F}_p,</math> satisfying the basic aim of defining a simple additive structure.

For <math>c_2</math> this step can be cumbersome. Write

:<math>c_1=c_1^p\equiv\left(a_1+b_1-a_0^{p-1}b_0-\frac{p-1}{2}a_0^{p-2}b_0^2-\cdots-a_0b_0^{p-1}\right)^p\bmod p^2</math>.

Just as for <math>c_0</math>, a single <math>p</math>th power is not enough: one must take

:<math>c_0=c_0^{p^2}\equiv(a_0+b_0)^{p^2} \bmod p^3.</math>

However, <math>\binom{p^2}{i}</math> is not in general divisible by <math>p^2</math>, but it is divisible when <math>i=pd</math>, in which case <math>a^ib^{p^2-i}=a^db^{p-d}</math> combined with similar monomials in <math>c_1^p</math> will make a multiple of <math>p^2</math>.

At this step, one works with addition of the form

:<math>\begin{align}
c_0 &\equiv a_0+b_0 && \bmod p \\
c_0^p+c_1 p &\equiv a_0^p+a_1 p+b_0^p+b_1 p && \bmod p^2 \\
c_0^{p^2}+c_1^p p+c_2 p^2 &\equiv a_0^{p^2}+a_1^p p+a_2 p^2+b_0^{p^2}+b_1^p p+b_2 p^2 && \bmod p^3
\end{align}</math>

This motivates the definition of Witt vectors.

==Construction of Witt rings==
Fix a prime number ''p''. A '''Witt vector'''<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Illusie|first=Luc|author-link=Luc Illusie|date=1979|title=Complexe de de Rham-Witt et cohomologie cristalline|url=http://www.numdam.org/item/ASENS_1979_4_12_4_501_0/|journal=Annales scientifiques de l'École Normale Supérieure|language=fr|volume=12|issue=4|pages=501–661|doi=10.24033/asens.1374|doi-access=free}}</ref> over a commutative ring <math>R</math> (relative to the prime <math>p</math>) is a sequence <math>(X_0,X_1,X_2,\ldots)</math> of elements of <math>R</math>. The '''Witt polynomials''' <math>W_i</math> can be defined by 
#<math> W_0=X_0</math>
#<math> W_1=X_0^p+pX_1</math>
#<math> W_2=X_0^{p^2}+pX_1^p+p^2X_2</math>
and in general
:<math> W_n=\sum_{i=0}^np^iX_i^{p^{n-i}}</math>.

The <math>W_n</math> are called the '''ghost components''' of the Witt vector <math>(X_0,X_1,X_2,\ldots)</math>, and are usually denoted by <math>X^{(n)}</math>; taken together, the <math>W_n</math> define the '''ghost map''' to <math display="inline">\prod_{i=0}^\infty R</math>. If <math display="inline">R</math> is ''p''-torsionfree, then the ghost map is [[injective]] and the ghost components can be thought of as an alternative coordinate system for the <math>R</math>-[[module (mathematics)|module]] of sequences (though note that the ghost map is not [[surjective]] unless <math display="inline">R</math> is ''p''-divisible). 

The '''ring of''' ('''''p''-typical''') '''Witt vectors''' <math>W(R)</math> is defined by componentwise addition and multiplication of the ghost components. That is, that there is a unique way to make the set of Witt vectors over any commutative ring <math>R</math> into a ring such that:

# the sum and product are given by polynomials with integer coefficients that do not depend on <math>R</math>, and
# projection to each ghost component is a ring homomorphism from the Witt vectors over <math>R</math>'','' to <math>R</math>.

In other words, 

*<math>(X+Y)_i</math> and <math>(XY)_i</math> are given by polynomials with integer coefficients that do not depend on ''R'', and

*<math>X^{(i)}+Y^{(i)} = (X+Y)^{(i)}</math> and <math>X^{(i)}Y^{(i)} = (XY)^{(i)}.</math>

The first few polynomials giving the sum and product of Witt vectors can be written down explicitly. For example, 

:<math>(X_0,X_1,\ldots)+(Y_0,Y_1,\ldots)=(X_0+Y_0, X_1+Y_1-((X_0+Y_0)^p - X_0^p -Y_0^p)/p,\ldots)</math>
:<math>(X_0,X_1,\ldots)\times(Y_0,Y_1,\ldots)=(X_0 Y_0, X_0^p Y_1+X_1 Y_0^p+p X_1 Y_1,\ldots)</math>

These are to be understood as shortcuts for the actual formulas: if for example the ring <math>R</math> has characteristic <math>p</math>, the division by <math>p</math> in the first formula above, the one by <math>p^2</math> that would appear in the next component and so forth, do not make sense. However, if the <math>p</math>-power of the sum is developed, the terms <math>X_0^p+Y_0^p</math> are cancelled with the previous ones and the remaining ones are simplified by <math>p</math>, no division by <math>p</math> remains and the formula makes sense. The same consideration applies to the ensuing components.

=== Examples of addition and multiplication ===
As would be expected, the [[identity element]] in the ring of Witt vectors <math>W(A)</math> is the element<blockquote><math>\underline{1} = (1,0,0,\ldots)</math></blockquote>Adding this element to itself gives a non-trivial sequence, for example in <math>W(\mathbb{F}_5)</math>,<blockquote><math>\underline{1} + \underline{1} = (2,4,\ldots)</math></blockquote>since<blockquote><math>\begin{align}
2 &= 1 + 1\\
4 &= -\frac{32 - 1 - 1}{5} \mod 5 \\
&\cdots
\end{align}</math></blockquote>which is not the expected behavior, since it doesn't equal <math>\underline{2}</math>. But, when the map <math>m:W(\mathbb{F}_5) \to \mathbb{F}_5</math> is reduced with, one gets <math>m(\omega(1) + \omega(1)) = m(\omega(2))</math>. Note if there is an element <math>x \in A</math> and an element <math>a \in W(A)</math>, then<blockquote><math>\underline{x}a = (xa_0,x^pa_1,\ldots,x^{p^n}a_n,\ldots)</math></blockquote>showing that multiplication also behaves in a highly non-trivial manner.

==Examples==
* The Witt ring of any commutative ring <math>R</math> in which <math>p</math> is invertible, is isomorphic to <math>R^\N</math> (the product of a countable number of copies of <math>R</math>). The Witt polynomials always give a homomorphism from the ring of Witt vectors to <math>R^\N</math>, and if <math>p</math> is invertible this homomorphism is an isomorphism.
* The Witt ring <math>W(\mathbb{F}_p) \cong \mathbb{Z}_p</math> of the finite field of order <math>p</math> is the ring of <math>p</math>-adic integers written in terms of the Teichmüller representatives, as demonstrated above.
* The Witt ring <math>W(\mathbb{F}_q) \cong \mathcal{O}_K</math> of a finite field of order <math>p^n</math> is the [[ring of integers]] of the unique [[Splitting of prime ideals in Galois extensions|unramified extension]] of degree <math>n</math> of the ring of <math>p</math>-adic numbers <math>K/\mathbb{Q}_p</math>. Note <math>K \cong \mathbb{Q}_p(\mu_{q-1})</math> for <math>\mu_{q-1}</math> the <math>(q-1)</math>-st root of unity, hence <math>W(\mathbb{F}_q) \cong \mathbb{Z}_p[\mu_{q-1}]</math>.
* The truncated Witt ring <math>W_{n+1}(\mathbb{F}_p[t])</math> can be described as<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Illusie|first=Luc|date=1979|title=Complexe de de Rham-Witt et cohomologie cristalline|location=Section I.2.B|url=http://www.numdam.org/item/ASENS_1979_4_12_4_501_0/|journal=Annales scientifiques de l'École Normale Supérieure|language=fr|volume=12|issue=4|pages=501–661|doi=10.24033/asens.1374|doi-access=free}}</ref>  
<blockquote>
<math>
\begin{array}{rcl}
W_{n+1}(\mathbb{F}_p[t])
&\cong&
\left \{ 
\sum a_i t^{i/p^n}  
\in 
(\mathbb{Z}/p^{n+1})[t^{1/p^n}]
\ :\ 
p i a_i = 0 
\ 
\textrm{ mod } 
\ 
p^{n+1}
\right \} \\
&=&
(\mathbb{Z}/p^n)[t] + p(\mathbb{Z}/p^n)[t^{1/p}] + p^2(\mathbb{Z}/p^n)[t^{1/p^2}] + \dots + p^n(\mathbb{Z}/p^n)[t^{1/p^n}]
\end{array}
</math>
</blockquote>
The Witt vectors are the inverse limit along the canonical projections <blockquote>
<math>W(\mathbb{F}_p[t]) = \lim (\dots \to W_{n+1}(\mathbb{F}_p[t]) \to W_{n}(\mathbb{F}_p[t]) \to \dots \to W_1(\mathbb{F}_p[t]) = \mathbb{F}_p[t]).</math></blockquote>
Here the transition homomorphisms are induced by reduction <math>(\mathbb{Z}/p^{n+1})[t^{1/p^n}] \to (\mathbb{Z}/p^{n})[t^{1/p^n}]</math>.

==Universal Witt vectors==
The Witt polynomials for different primes <math>p</math> are special cases of universal Witt polynomials, which can be used to form a universal Witt ring (not depending on a choice of prime <math>p</math>). Define the universal Witt polynomials <math>W_n</math> for <math>n\geq1</math> by 
#<math> W_1=X_1</math>
#<math> W_2=X_1^2+2X_2</math>
#<math> W_3=X_1^3+3X_3</math>
#<math> W_4=X_1^{4}+2X_2^2+4X_4</math>
and in general
:<math> W_n=\sum_{d|n}dX_d^{n/d}</math>.

Again, <math>(W_1,W_2,W_3,\ldots)</math> is called the vector of '''ghost components''' of the Witt vector <math>(X_1,X_2,X_3,\ldots)</math>, and is usually denoted by <math> (X^{(1)},X^{(2)},X^{(3)},\ldots)</math>.

These polynomials can be used to define the '''ring of universal Witt vectors''' or '''big Witt ring''' of any commutative ring <math>R</math> in much the same way as above (so the universal Witt polynomials are all homomorphisms to the ring <math>R</math>).

==Generating functions==
Witt also provided another approach using [[generating function]]s.<ref>{{cite book |last=Lang |first=Serge |title=Algebra |url=https://archive.org/details/undergraduatealg00lang_077 |url-access=limited |publisher=Springer|edition = 3rd |date=September 19, 2005 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/undergraduatealg00lang_077/page/n340 330] |chapter=Chapter VI: Galois Theory |isbn=978-0-387-95385-4}}</ref>

===Definition===
Let <math>X</math> be a Witt vector and define

:<math>f_X(t)=\prod_{n\ge 1}(1-X_n t^n)=\sum_{n\ge 0}A_n t^n</math>

For <math>n\ge 1</math> let <math>\mathcal{I}_n</math> denote the collection of subsets of <math>\{1,2,\ldots,n\}</math> whose elements add up to <math>n</math>. Then 

:<math>A_n=\sum_{I\in\mathcal{I}_n}(-1)^{|I|}\prod_{i\in I}{X_i}.</math>

One can get the ghost components by taking the [[logarithmic derivative]]:

:<math>\begin{align}
-t\frac{d}{dt}\log f_X(t)&= -t\frac{d}{dt} \sum_{n\ge 1} \log(1-X_n t^n) \\
&=t \frac{d}{dt}\sum_{n\ge 1}\sum_{d\ge 1}\frac{X_n^d t^{nd}}{d}\\
&=\sum_{n\ge 1}\sum_{d\ge 1} n X_n^d t^{nd} \\
&=\sum_{m\ge 1}\sum_{d|m}dX_{d}^{m/d}t^m \\
&=\sum_{m\ge 1}X^{(m)}t^m
\end{align}</math>

===Sum===
Now one can see <math>f_{Z}(t)=f_X(t) f_Y(t)</math> if <math>Z=X+Y</math>. So that 

:<math>C_n=\sum_{0\le i\le n}A_n B_{n-i},</math>

if <math>A_n,B_n,C_n</math> are the respective coefficients in the power series <math>f_X(t),f_Y(t),f_Z(t)</math>. Then 

:<math>Z_n=\sum_{0\le i\le n}A_n B_{n-i}-\sum_{I\in\mathcal{I}_n,I\ne\{n\}}(-1)^{|I|}\prod_{i\in I}{Z_i}.</math>

Since <math>A_n</math> is a polynomial in <math>X_1, \ldots, X_n</math> and likewise for <math>B_n</math>, one can show by [[mathematical induction|induction]] that <math>Z_n</math> is a polynomial in <math>X_1, \ldots, X_n, Y_1, \ldots, Y_n.</math>

===Product===
If <math>W=XY</math> is set, then

:<math>-t\frac{d}{dt}\log f_W(t)=-\sum_{m\ge 1}X^{(m)}Y^{(m)}t^m</math>.

but

:<math>\sum_{m\ge 1}X^{(m)}Y^{(m)}t^m=\sum_{m\ge 1}\sum_{d|m}d X_d^{m/d}\sum_{e|m}e Y_e^{m/e}t^m</math>.

Now 3-tuples <math>{m,d,e}</math> with <math>m \in \Z^+, d \,|\, m, e \,|\, m</math> are in bijection with 3-tuples <math>{d,e,n}</math> with <math>d,e,n \in \Z^+</math>, via <math>n = m/[d,e]</math> (<math>[d,e]</math> is the [[least common multiple]]), the series becomes

:<math>\sum_{d,e\ge 1}d e\sum_{n\ge 1} \left (X_d^{\frac{[d,e]}{d}} Y_e^{\frac{[d,e]}{e}} t^{[d,e]} \right )^n=-t\frac{d}{dt}\log\prod_{d,e\ge 1} \left (1-X_d^{\frac{[d,e]}{d}}Y_e^{\frac{[d,e]}{e}} t^{[d,e]} \right )^{\frac{de}{[d,e]}}</math>

so that 

:<math>f_W(t)=\prod_{d,e\ge 1} \left (1-X_d^{\frac{[d,e]}{d}}Y_e^{\frac{[d,e]}{e}} t^{[d,e]} \right )^{\frac{de}{[d,e]}}=\sum_{n\ge 0}D_n t^n</math>,

where <math>D_n</math> are polynomials of <math>X_1, \ldots, X_n, Y_1, \ldots, Y_n.</math> So by similar induction, 

:<math>f_W(t)=\prod_{n\ge 1}(1-W_n t^n),</math> 

then <math>W_n</math> can be solved as polynomials of <math>X_1,\ldots, X_n, Y_1,\ldots, Y_n</math>.

==Ring schemes==
The map taking a commutative ring <math>R</math> to the ring of Witt vectors over <math>R</math> (for a fixed prime <math>p</math>) is a [[functor]] from commutative rings to commutative rings, and is also [[representable functor|representable]], so it can be thought of as a [[scheme (mathematics)|ring scheme]], called the '''Witt scheme''', over <math>\operatorname{Spec}(\Z).</math> The Witt scheme can be canonically identified with the spectrum of the [[ring of symmetric functions]].

Similarly, the rings of truncated Witt vectors, and the rings of universal Witt vectors correspond to ring schemes, called the '''truncated Witt schemes''' and the '''universal Witt scheme'''.

Moreover, the functor taking the commutative ring <math>R</math> to the set <math>R^n</math> is represented by the [[affine space]] <math>\mathbb{A}_{\Z}^n</math>, and the ring structure on <math>R^n</math> makes <math>\mathbb{A}_{\Z}^n</math> into a ring scheme denoted <math>\underline{\mathcal{O}}^n</math>. From the construction of truncated Witt vectors, it follows that their associated ring scheme <math>\mathbb{W}_n</math> is the scheme <math>\mathbb{A}_{\Z}^n</math> with the unique ring structure such that the morphism <math>\mathbb{W}_n\to \underline{\mathcal{O}}^n</math> given by the Witt polynomials is a morphism of ring schemes.

==Commutative unipotent algebraic groups==

Over an [[algebraically closed field]] of characteristic 0, any [[unipotent]] abelian connected [[algebraic group]] is isomorphic to a product of copies of the additive group <math>G_a</math>. The analogue of this for fields of characteristic <math>p</math> is false: the truncated Witt schemes are [[counterexample]]s. (They are made into algebraic groups by using the additive structure instead of multiplication.) However, these are essentially the only counterexamples: over an algebraically closed field of characteristic <math>p</math>, any unipotent abelian connected algebraic group is [[Isogeny#Abelian varieties up to isogeny|isogenous]] to a product of truncated [[Witt group]] schemes.

== Universal property ==
[[André Joyal]] explicated the [[universal property]] of the (''p''-typical) Witt vectors.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Joyal |first=André |date=1985 |title=δ-anneaux et vecteurs de Witt |journal=C.R. Math. Rep. Acad. Sci. Canada |volume=7 |issue=3 |pages=177-182}}</ref> The basic intuition is that the formation of Witt vectors is the universal way to deform a characteristic ''p'' ring to characteristic 0 together with a lift of its Frobenius endomorphism.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Is there a universal property for Witt vectors? |url=https://mathoverflow.net/questions/58/is-there-a-universal-property-for-witt-vectors |access-date=2022-09-06 |website=MathOverflow |language=en}}</ref> To make this precise, define a '''<math>\delta</math>-ring''' <math display="inline">(R, \delta)</math> to consist of a commutative ring <math display="inline">R</math> together with a map of sets <math display="inline">\delta: R \to R</math> that is a [[p-derivation|''p''-derivation]], so that <math display="inline">\delta</math> satisfies the relations

* <math>\delta(0) = \delta(1) = 0</math>;
* <math>\delta(x y) = x^p \delta(y) + y^p \delta(x) + p \delta(x) \delta(y)</math>;
* <math>\delta(x + y) = \delta(x) + \delta(y) + \frac{x^p+y^p-(x+y)^p}{p}</math>.

The definition is such that given a <math>\delta</math>-ring <math display="inline">(R, \delta)</math>, if one defines the map <math display="inline">\phi: R \to R</math> by the formula <math display="inline">\phi(x) = x^p + p \delta(x)</math>, then <math display="inline">\phi</math> is a ring homomorphism lifting Frobenius on <math>R/p</math>. Conversely, if <math display="inline">R</math> is ''p''-torsionfree, then this formula uniquely defines the structure of a <math>\delta</math>-ring on <math display="inline">R</math> from that of a Frobenius lift. One may thus regard the notion of <math>\delta</math>-ring as a suitable replacement for a Frobenius lift in the non-''p''-torsionfree case.

The collection of <math>\delta</math>-rings and ring homomorphisms thereof respecting the <math>\delta</math>-structure assembles to a [[Category (mathematics)|category]] <math display="inline">\mathrm{CRing}_{\delta}</math>. One then has a [[forgetful functor]]<math display="block">U: \mathrm{CRing}_{\delta} \to \mathrm{CRing}</math>whose [[right adjoint]] identifies with the functor <math display="inline">W</math> of Witt vectors. The functor <math display="inline">U</math> creates [[limits and colimits]] and admits an explicitly describable left adjoint as a type of [[Free object#Free functor|free functor]]; from this, it can be shown that <math display="inline">\mathrm{CRing}_{\delta}</math> inherits [[Accessible category#κ-accessible and locally presentable categories|local presentability]] from <math>\mathrm{CRing}</math> so that one can construct the functor <math display="inline">W</math> by appealing to the [[Formal criteria for adjoint functors|adjoint functor theorem]].

One further has that <math display="inline">W</math> restricts to a [[fully faithful functor]] on the [[full subcategory]] of [[perfect field|perfect rings]] of characteristic ''p''. Its image then consists of those <math>\delta</math>-rings that are perfect (in the sense that the associated map <math display="inline">\phi</math> is an isomorphism) and whose underlying ring is ''p''-adically complete.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Bhatt |first=Bhargav |author-link=Bhargav Bhatt (mathematician) |date=October 8, 2018 |title=Lecture II: Delta rings |url=https://www.math.ias.edu/~bhatt/teaching/prismatic-columbia/lecture2-delta-rings.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220906153816/https://www.math.ias.edu/~bhatt/teaching/prismatic-columbia/lecture2-delta-rings.pdf |archive-date=September 6, 2022}}</ref>
